name: Biomarker tracking (DunedinPACE)

card.summary: Tracking aging scores such as DunedinPACE and blood markers over time to see whether diet, training and sleep habits are slowing biological aging, which people link to looking younger.
card.note: Epigenetic clocks are research tools; consumer test results vary and their link to appearance is not established.

quick.overview:
Biomarker tracking means periodically measuring health markers, including DNA-methylation aging scores such as DunedinPACE, and watching how they change. Longevity-minded people use the scores as a feedback loop for lifestyle choices they connect to looking and feeling younger.

DunedinPACE is described in an eLife paper as a DNA methylation biomarker of the pace of aging, meaning it estimates how fast a person is aging rather than their age. Randomized trials have begun to test whether interventions such as omega-3, exercise or calorie restriction shift such clocks.
quick.how: Users order a blood or saliva-based epigenetic test, record the result, and repeat after a period of changed habits, sometimes sharing their numbers publicly in biomarker-tracking communities. They typically pair it with routine blood panels.
quick.risks: The scores are probabilistic research measures. Epigenetic clocks are noted to reflect an emergent property of the epigenome rather than a proven cause of aging, and lifestyle factors show only weak associations with age acceleration in blood. Results can fluctuate between tests, and public sharing of health data has privacy implications.

lead: Biomarker tracking, in the longevity corner of looksmaxxing culture, is the practice of repeatedly measuring aging scores and health markers and publishing or comparing them. DunedinPACE is the best-known example of a pace-of-aging score; it is a DNA methylation biomarker described in the journal eLife in 2022 [1].

Epigenetic clocks estimate biological age from age-related changes in DNA methylation. The first multi-tissue clock was published by Steve Horvath in 2013, and later clocks such as PhenoAge and GrimAge add phenotypic and mortality information [2]. Age acceleration, the gap between estimated and chronological age, suggests faster or slower aging than expected [2].

The link to looks is by the chain people describe: habits like training, sleep and nutrition that slow aging scores are also habits associated with skin quality and physique. Studies have not established a direct relationship between a clock score and appearance.

chain: Measure aging score and blood markers
Habits that may support a younger-looking appearance
angle.text: Tracking gives numbers to a goal of aging more slowly, which people associate with a younger look. The score itself does not change appearance; it is used as feedback on habits.

paras: An epigenetic clock is a biomarker of aging estimating biological age from DNA methylation at CpG sites [2]. Horvath's 2013 clock used 353 CpG sites across tissues [2]. DunedinPACE differs in being framed as a measure of the pace of aging rather than an age estimate [1].

Studies have linked DunedinPACE-style pace-of-aging measures to health outcomes: a Neurology study examined association of blood-based pace of aging with cognitive impairment and dementia [3], and a PNAS study in a representative sample of older Americans examined associations of epigenetic age acceleration with morbidity and mortality [4]. A twin study examined adolescent lifestyle habits and biological aging [5].

Overviews note that clock CpGs likely have no causal effect, that clocks may detect treatments changing the future rate of aging but not single-moment effects, that accuracy depends to some extent on the DNA source, and that lifestyle factors have weak associations with age acceleration in blood [2].

In the DO-HEALTH randomized trial post hoc analysis of 777 participants over three years, omega-3 alone slowed PhenoAge, GrimAge2 and DunedinPACE, with standardized effects equivalent to roughly 2.9 to 3.8 months, and the researchers described a small protective effect [6]. The CALERIE trial examined long-term calorie restriction on DNA methylation measures of biological aging [7]. No studies found testing whether DunedinPACE changes correspond to changes in facial or physical appearance.

timeline.event: Horvath publishes the first multi-tissue epigenetic clock [2].
